Antigone. Sophocles' tragedy about defiance, duty, and the collision between familial piety and political law. Set after the civil war in Thebes, Antigone faces an impossible choice: bury her brother Polynices, who died as a traitor, or obey Creon's decree forbidding it under pain of death.

Antigone's brothers, Eteocles and Polynices, killed each other fighting over Thebes. Creon, now ruling, sees Polynices as a traitor and makes his stance absolute: any citizen who buries him will die. For Antigone, though, family duty runs deeper than any political order. She buries her brother with ritual and is discovered.

Creon condemns her to be entombed alive. His son Haemon, betrothed to Antigone, begs his father to spare her, but Creon refuses. When the blind prophet Tiresias warns him that his rigidity has angered the gods, Creon finally relents. It's too late. Antigone has already taken her own life in the tomb. Haemon, discovering her body, kills himself beside her in grief.

The tragedy ripples outward. Creon's wife Eurydice, learning of her son's death, kills herself as well. Creon is left with nothing—his family destroyed, his authority hollow. The play asks an urgent question that still matters: must we always obey the law of the state, or do we owe something higher to our blood, to the gods, to our conscience?
